To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

feeding hens in early laying in energy diluted diets with high NSP content or by adding insoluble NSP to the diets, resulted in higher feed intake and similar egg performance compared to the undilated diet.

feeding energy diluted diets to hens in early laying results in a higher feed intake and a similar energy intake, egg production and weight gain compared to feeding the undiluted diet, when sand or grit is added to the diet (low NSP diets) or when the diet contains a high amount of non starch polysacchrides (high NSP diets).
feeding low or high non starch polysaccha-rides (NSP) diets, in combination with sand or grit, resulted in higher feed intake and similar or better egg performance compared with undiluted diets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of dietary dilution with insoluble non-starch polysaccharides on the feed intake, egg performance and body weight of hens in the first 3 months after the onset of lay.
the effect of dietary dilution on feed consumption and eating time of laying hens.
the effect of feed form and particle size distribution of insoluble NSP on feed intake, feed form, particle size distribution and egg performance of hens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of NSP in the diets of hens in the early laying phase is not beneficial, but the use of NSPs is a promising tool to reduce the risk of feather pecking.

the hens in early laying were able to compensate the effect of energy dilution by increasing feed intake, but only when the NSP concentration of the diet was high enough (128 g/kg) and the particle size distribution was coarse (fine fraction < 10 g/kg).
the effect of dietary dilution on feed efficiency and egg production of hens in the laying period can be compensated for by increasing the feed intake, but the energy intake remains unchanged.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hens were able to compensate the dilution of the control diet by 10% with either sand or grit addition to the low NSP diet and by adding NSP to the high NSP diets.
hens can compensate for 10 to 20% dietary energy dilution by increasing feed intake, but this compensation is limited by the amount of NSP present in the diet.

the use of energy diluted diets, supplemented with sand and grit, NSP rich raw material or insoluble NSP, is an effective tool in reducing feed intake, eating behaviour and feather pecking in laying hens in the early laying period.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hens in the early laying stage are able to adapt to a wide range of diets and can be used to test the effects of different dietary ingredients and feeding practices on performance.
hens in the early laying phase are able to compensate for dietary dilution with sand, grit, or insoluble NSP.
the hens are able to compensate for energy dilution in the diet.
